demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I feel isolated and set apart from others
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Physical pain in the same body parts as during the event is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being an unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, unless the patient was also physically injured during the event. That makes this item clinically implausible from the provided trauma context.

A global mistrust appraisal is a weak fit with bereavement trauma unless there is some interpersonal betrayal, negligence, or assault-related context. The rest of the profile centers on loss, alarm, and isolation rather than interpersonal threat from other people, so this item is not well supported by the trauma type or the other selected items.

For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, ambulances can plausibly cue the death context and workplace cues may be idiosyncratically linked, but 'People cycling' is hard to connect clinically unless the loved one died in a cycling-related incident, which is not reflected anywhere else in threat, appraisals, or memory. It stands out as a trigger with no supporting context in the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: The memory profile is dominated by grief-related recall and affective reliving without clear imagery, which fits bereavement trauma. 'Intense shame' on recall is not impossible, but here it lacks support from the negative appraisals, which focus on identity loss, isolation, and life destruction rather than self-blame, guilt, or humiliation. In this profile, shame is insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and trauma type.

vignette: Kofi had always taken pride in his work as a painter, transforming drab spaces into vibrant masterpieces that brought joy to those who inhabited them. But since the sudden loss of his younger brother, Kwame, everything about his job felt tainted. The smell of fresh paint now reminded him of the hospital room where he had last seen his brother's lifeless body. The sound of sirens outside his workplace made Kofi's heart skip a beat, transporting him back to that fateful night when an ambulance had rushed Kwame to the hospital. In the months following the loss, Kofi found himself increasingly on edge at work. He would catch himself scanning the room for potential dangers, as if expecting some unseen threat to emerge from the shadows. His coworkers noticed a change in him, too - he was more irritable and withdrawn than before. When they tried to offer condolences or talk about their own experiences with loss, Kofi would shut down, feeling like an outsider looking in on conversations that only served as painful reminders of his own grief. At home, the tension didn't dissipate. Kofi's wife, Ama, would often try to initiate conversations about Kwame, hoping to process her own emotions and support her husband. But Kofi would become overwhelmed by the sheer force of his feelings - a crushing wave of sadness that seemed to arrive unannounced, without warning or visual memory to anchor it. He began to withdraw from social interactions altogether, feeling like an outsider in his own community. Nighttime was the worst. As he lay awake, his body felt coiled and ready to spring into action at a moment's notice. His mind would replay the events leading up to Kwame's death, searching for some clue or warning sign that might have prevented the tragedy. The darkness seemed to amplify every creak of the house, every distant siren, until Kofi was convinced that danger lurked around every corner. As time went on, these hypervigilant episodes took their toll on his relationships and daily routines. Ama grew concerned about Kofi's increasing isolation, his inability to sleep or focus on even the simplest tasks. His painting business began to suffer as well - missed deadlines, botched jobs, and a general lack of enthusiasm that repelled clients. Kofi couldn't shake the feeling that he was losing himself in the aftermath of Kwame's death. He felt disconnected from his own life, like an observer watching someone else struggle to cope with an unbearable burden. The memories of his brother still lingered, frozen images that replayed in his mind without context or narrative thread. It was only when Kofi realized he couldn't face another sleepless night, another day of pretending to be the man he used to be, that he finally reached out for help. He knew it wouldn't be easy - confronting the pain and grief head-on would require more courage than he'd ever shown before. But with Ama by his side, urging him forward, Kofi took a tentative step into the unknown, hoping against hope that somehow, someway, he might rediscover himself amidst the wreckage of his shattered world.
